raw.assessment: The incumbent supplies removable, preassembled compartments but misses the observed time target (11-minute median); seven of ten observed customers achieved their arrangement unaided. Five missing/incorrect-part reports signal a completeness problem without establishing five independently verified packing errors. Repeated three-compartment orders taking seven to nine minutes limit any claim that assembly is uniformly too slow: all six extreme delays occurred in mixed batches. This supports investigating variation handling, although layout complexity remains confounded. Overlapping widths also limit a simple partition-width explanation for insertion retries.

openings.claim: Switching layouts may increase selection and checking work; staging the exact components against each order slip before insertion could reduce omissions and delays.
openings.delta: Explains a potentially avoidable portion of mixed-batch delays while retaining full assembly and customer rearrangeability.
openings.prediction: For the same layout mix, staged selection reduces selection/checking time and component discrepancies; insertion time need not improve.
openings.probe: Use spare-board samples for matched rehearsals by both workers, alternating current and staged selection with the same layout sequence. Separately time selection, insertion, checking and packing, including staging overhead; verify component counts and exterior color against slips. Use existing bench space and slips. Stop before rehearsals threaten the delivery date.
assumptions: Existing slips identify required components accurately.
Rehearsals fit available working time; repeated samples provide directional evidence only.

openings.claim: Does identifying the short partition on an order-specific diagram resolve customer placement difficulty without changing the hardware?
openings.delta: Separates a guidance problem from persistent physical insertion difficulty.
openings.prediction: If guidance is responsible, diagram cues reduce location questions and improve unaided arrangement while insertion retry frequency remains similar.
openings.probe: Randomly assign the ten willing participants to existing versus annotated existing diagrams with identical complete parts. Record placement questions, insertion retries and correct unaided arrangement within ten minutes. Count annotation time in workshop totals; treat this small comparison as exploratory.
assumptions: Existing diagram stock can be annotated without added material expense.

raw.assessment: The current process misses the time target; the small unpacking sample also falls below the unaided-arrangement target. Missing-part reports do not establish verified shortages, and overlapping widths leave insertion difficulties unexplained. Both alternatives below are hypotheses requiring resource and outcome checks.

openings.claim: An order-specific removable packing carrier could double as an assembly map: each loose partition occupies a labeled position corresponding to its destination, while the exterior frame remains assembled. Empty carrier positions would expose omissions before sealing.
openings.delta: Replace workshop partition insertion and the generic three-layout diagram with a physical transfer guide tied to the selected arrangement.
openings.prediction: Workshop insertion time falls, short-part placement questions decrease, and missing pieces become visible during packing; added carrier preparation could erase those gains.
openings.probe: Use spare board for five carrier samples and five current-format samples with identical component requirements. Assign the ten participants between formats, balancing layouts. Record total workshop time including carrier preparation, verified contents, unaided arrangement, and material cost. Use remaining samples for fit and packing checks before considering the fixed-date pilot.
assumptions: A carrier can stay within both spending caps and the delivery date.
Frame dimensions, stationery capacity, selected counts, and exterior color are preserved.

openings.claim: Do difficult insertions follow a particular partition, a particular base slot, or their pairing?
openings.delta: Treat insertion as a compatibility problem rather than infer that partition width alone explains rework.
openings.prediction: Persistent difficulty across slots implicates the partition; across partitions it implicates the slot; difficulty restricted to particular combinations suggests an interaction.
openings.probe: On spare samples, cross-swap matching partition types among compatible slots and record first-attempt success, orientation, and insertion time. Counterbalance order and repeat on fresh samples to distinguish compatibility from loosening through repeated use. Separately time insertion during normal work to estimate its contribution to the three-minute gap.
assumptions: Sampling does not delay accepted orders.
Compatible slot-part combinations can be tested without altering compartment counts or capacity.

critiques.assumption: Moving partition insertion to customers saves workshop time without lowering unaided arrangement success.
critiques.limitation: D2-O5 establishes insertion retries, but neither their customer impact nor their time contribution is measured. A destination map addresses placement while leaving mechanical difficulty intact. A2 diagnoses compatibility but does not specify how its result should change fulfillment.
critiques.opening: Use compatibility evidence to decide which insertion tasks may be transferred to customers, preserving workshop assembly for difficult combinations.
critiques.comparison: A1 transfers insertion broadly; A2 investigates its causes. Their interaction could selectively transfer easy insertion tasks. It fails if sample performance does not predict customer performance or sorting and carrier preparation consume the savings.
critiques.probe: On fresh samples, screen compatible combinations, then test customer insertion and total workshop time before choosing any fulfillment format.

critiques.assumption: Staged or visibly occupied positions establish correct order contents.
critiques.limitation: A wrong partition can occupy a position; D2-O3 includes incorrect-part reports. Empty-position detection alone cannot establish correctness.
critiques.opening: Verify partition identity as well as occupancy against the original order slip.
critiques.comparison: This adds a correctness check to both staging and carrier use; a wrongly translated order template remains a shared failure source.
critiques.probe: Seed a wrong-type substitution in rehearsal and check whether workers detect it without prompting.

openings.claim: A compatibility-screened partial-assembly policy could retain difficult insertions in the workshop while transferring candidate easy insertions through A1's map carrier, with Z1 staging and explicit type checks.
openings.delta: Allocates individual insertion tasks by assessed difficulty instead of choosing one assembly format for every order.
openings.prediction: Compared with A1, customer retries may fall; compared with A2 alone, diagnosis changes labor allocation; compared with Z1, workshop insertion may decrease. Gains disappear if classification or carrier overhead dominates.
openings.probe: Allocate at most 15 samples across fresh compatibility screening and matched fulfillment rehearsals. Use ten participants for an exploratory comparison with full assembly. Include screening, sorting, checking and carrier preparation in costs and time; verify contents, capacity, color and unaided arrangement. This does not establish pilot targets.
openings.fit: Preserves outcome and constraints only if budget, footprint, rearrangeability and fixed-date checks pass.
assumptions: Screening predicts customer difficulty sufficiently to justify a later pilot.
Rehearsals fit the delivery schedule; all probes remain proposed.
